body: The caching trade-off is real. We ended up putting React Query on top of tRPC just to claw back some of what we lost from HTTP caching.
Curious how you're handling public-facing endpoints - did you keep those on REST or go full tRPC there too?
Kept REST for anything public - tRPC's coupling to a TS client isn't worth it once you don't control who's calling the API.
The memo here is that Promise.all is not a magic fix if one routine stalls forever.
I keep a tiny helper to wrap each task in a timeout so the failure mode stays obvious.
This is exactly the kind of tool I end up writing in a side quest and then never shipping.
The best scaffolds feel opinionated without feeling heavy.
The hidden cost of a shared queue is that the leak only shows up under exactly the right churn pattern.
Did you use heap snapshots to confirm the listeners were being retained, or did the listener count give you enough evidence?
Heap snapshots confirmed it. The listener count was what made me start looking in that direction.
The ransom note description is painfully accurate. At some point I stop reading the classes and just start guessing.
I usually extract the component before I reach for @apply too. Makes the responsive variants much easier to reason about.
I've found that a long class list isn't necessarily bad if the component is tiny. It's when the same 15 classes show up in five places that I get nervous.
Exactly. Duplication is sometimes less painful than inventing an abstraction just to shorten the HTML.
The fact that the bug only appeared after switching tabs a few times is classic subscription cleanup territory.
React Strict Mode actually caught something similar for me. Seeing the effect run twice finally made me check whether I was cleaning things up.
Same. I used to think the Strict Mode behavior was just annoying until it caught an actual lifecycle bug.
This is also why I prefer putting the cleanup immediately next to the setup. Much harder to forget what needs undoing.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE should honestly be one of the first things people learn before adding indexes.
The write overhead is the part I didn't appreciate either. Read performance gets all the attention because it's easier to demonstrate.
Also worth checking index size. I've inherited tables where the indexes took more space than the actual data.
That's exactly what happened to us. We had an index for a query that ran maybe twice a day.
Partial indexes have been useful for us when only a small subset of rows is queried regularly.
Yeah, indexing everything because 'we might query it' is a surprisingly expensive habit.
Shared types are probably my favorite part of TypeScript in full-stack projects.
Same. The compiler basically becomes another person checking that the frontend and backend are still speaking the same language.
Although I've definitely had TypeScript errors that were technically correct and still took me an hour to understand.
That's the tax. The compiler saves you from one class of bugs and occasionally introduces a new class of emotional damage.
SQLite is fantastic for local development. Being able to delete the database and recreate it in seconds is hard to beat.
Exactly. I think people sometimes jump to Postgres because it's what they expect a 'real' app to use.
The important question is what the workload actually needs. SQLite can take you surprisingly far.
Request IDs are one of those tiny things that suddenly make logs usable once you have concurrent requests.
I started doing this after accidentally debugging three users' requests at the same time. Never again.
Do you generate the request ID in Express or at the reverse proxy?
At the app layer for now. We also accept an incoming ID when the proxy provides one.
Container queries made cards so much easier to reuse. I don't have to keep asking what breakpoint the parent happens to be at.
The mental shift from viewport-first to component-first responsive design is the biggest part for me.
I still use media queries for page-level layout, but container queries are great for the actual components.
Same. I don't think they replace media queries, they just solve a different problem.
900MB to 200MB is a pretty serious reduction. What was taking up most of the original image?
Mostly dev dependencies and stuff copied from the project root that never needed to be in the runtime image.
Multi-stage builds are one of those Docker features that sounds complicated until you actually use one.
This is basically the difference between 'the API is fast' and 'the page feels fast'. They're not the same thing.
Skeleton loaders helped us too, but only after we stopped using one giant loading state for the whole page.
I've also started questioning whether every dashboard widget needs to load immediately. Some of them can wait until they're actually visible.
That's a good point. Lazy loading isn't just for images.
We actually had a similar handler and ended up losing the original stack trace because the error was logged after it had already been wrapped.
Generic client errors plus detailed server logs is the sweet spot. Users don't need to know your file paths.
Also worth making sure the error middleware is actually the last error-handling middleware in the chain. Learned that one the hard way.
The number of divs pretending to be buttons I've found in production is honestly concerning.
And then someone adds ```role="button"``` and thinks they've solved it.
Native elements are seriously underrated. The browser gives you keyboard behavior, focus behavior and semantics for free.
This is why I try to use ARIA as a last resort rather than the first solution.
Five minutes for a proper button beats an afternoon trying to make a div behave like one.
Failing at startup is so much better than finding out when someone hits the one endpoint that uses the missing variable.
We use a schema for env validation now. It also catches things like a port accidentally being treated as a string.
Do you validate optional variables too, or only the required ones?
Required ones at startup. Optional ones get defaults where that makes sense.
N+1 problems are especially nasty because the individual queries can all look completely harmless.
51 requests for 50 projects is the kind of thing that looks fine in development with five records.
Exactly. Small development datasets hide this stuff really well.
I usually check the browser network tab now whenever a page feels slow. It's amazing how quickly a list can turn into dozens of requests.
The first time I went back to a slow bundler after using Vite I thought something was broken.
Fast feedback definitely makes me more willing to try things. If every change takes ages, I start second guessing whether it's worth experimenting.
HMR alone is enough to make me not want to go back.
The merge conflict is usually just the final boss. The real problem started when nobody agreed on the interface.
This. Git can tell you that two things conflict, but it can't tell you what the team actually intended.
We've started putting API changes in the PR description before anyone starts the frontend work. Has helped a lot.
Documentation doesn't have to be huge either. Sometimes a five-line example response is enough.
Having migrations in Git completely changed how comfortable I am making schema changes.
Same. A fresh clone actually produces the same database now instead of relying on tribal knowledge.
The first migration I ever wrote felt like overkill. Six months later I couldn't imagine going back.
The important part is committing the migration files. A local migration that exists only on your machine doesn't help anybody.
The OPTIONS request confused me for way too long. I thought my frontend was somehow making an extra API call.
The network tab makes CORS issues much easier once you know to look for the preflight.
One thing that got me was custom headers. Suddenly a request I thought was simple started triggering a preflight.
Yep. Content-Type and custom headers can make the browser decide it needs to ask permission first.
I wish the browser error told you more clearly which origin and request header caused the block.
This is how a harmless boolean becomes technical debt. The original decision wasn't wrong, the requirements just changed.
I've started asking 'is this really one concept?' whenever a boolean starts accumulating exceptions.
Separate notification preferences also make the UI much easier to evolve later.
The giant JPEG hiding halfway down the page is almost always real.
Image compression has been one of the easiest performance wins I've found on content-heavy pages.
I also started checking actual image dimensions. Uploading a 4000px image for a 400px card is not doing anybody favors.
Modern formats help too. WebP cut the size of some of our assets without any visible difference.
Date and timezone bugs are exactly why I don't trust 'it's just a formatter' as an argument against testing.
Midnight bugs are especially evil because everything works perfectly until the date happens to cross the boundary.
I usually keep all timezone conversion in one place now. Makes it much easier to test.
The worst bugs are the ones where the test data happens to be nowhere near the edge case.
I needed this reminder. I've definitely built abstractions just because the duplicated code offended me.
There's a difference between duplication and repetition that actually needs to stay synchronized. I think we sometimes optimize for the wrong one.
The 'one utility function with 14 options' phase of every project is real.
I've started asking whether the abstraction makes the calling code easier to understand. If not, it probably isn't helping.
This is also why I don't mind a little duplication early in a project. You don't know the real shape of the code yet.
